name: Shoulder brace (Figure-8 clavicle)

lead: A figure-8 clavicle brace is a padded strap harness that crosses the upper back and loops over each shoulder, drawing the shoulders back. It was developed for collarbone (clavicle) fractures and is also sold as a posture corrector for rounded shoulders.

The appearance goal is a more upright stance: shoulders held back, chest more open, and a broader-looking upper frame while the brace is worn. Studies cover medical uses and brace comparisons rather than long-term cosmetic posture change.

paras: Users wear the brace over or under clothing for set periods, often alongside back and shoulder strengthening. Posture correctors in general are described as reminders that build awareness of current posture.

Comparisons for clavicle fractures report lower patient satisfaction with figure-8 bandages than with slings, attributed to discomfort and skin irritation. Tight straps can press on the underarm area, and fracture care should be directed by a clinician.

angle.text: While worn, the brace holds the shoulders in a retracted position, which changes how upright and broad the upper body looks. Some users pair it with strengthening exercises to carry the posture over when it is off.

lead: A figure-8 clavicle brace is a harness whose straps loop around each shoulder and cross at the back, holding the shoulders back. In medicine, the figure-of-eight splint is one of two common nonoperative options for clavicle fractures, the other being a simple arm sling; immobilization is mainly for pain relief.[1] Patent filings for 'clavicle brace' designs date back to the 1970s and 1980s.[2][3][4]

In appearance communities the same style of strap is used as a posture corrector: pulling the shoulders back counteracts rounded or forward shoulders and gives a more upright, open-chested line. Posture correctors in general are described as devices that lead to awareness of current posture.[5]

Research includes randomized trials of shoulder braces in different conditions, such as a 2020 crossover trial in people with shoulder impingement and rounded-shoulder posture, trials of figure-8 shoulder braces in chronic stroke rehabilitation, and a 2023 comparison of three wearable braces designed to correct rounded posture.[6][7][8][9]

paras: The figure-8 pattern places a strap across the upper back with loops over each shoulder, so that tightening it draws the shoulders posteriorly.[1] Medical versions are used to immobilize a fractured collarbone; posture versions are sold in neoprene or elastic with adjustable straps.[1][5]

Posture braces are marketed to people with rounded shoulders or desk-related slouching. Wikipedia's article on posture correctors says forms include braces, restrictive clothing and sensor devices, and that some sellers describe them as reminders rather than treatments.[5]

Wikipedia's clavicle-fracture article, citing a Cochrane review, states that the type of sling does not seem to affect healing and no functional difference has been reported between a figure-of-eight bandage and a sling, but satisfaction is lower with the figure-of-eight because of discomfort and skin irritation.[1]

For posture correctors in general, scientific evidence of effectiveness is described as limited and possibly biased because some manufacturers fund the research, and the article notes little evidence linking back pain to slouching.[5]

A 2020 randomized crossover trial examined the immediate effects of a shoulder brace on muscle activity and scapular kinematics in people with shoulder impingement and rounded-shoulder posture.[6] Randomized trials published in 2024-2025 tested 8-figure shoulder braces during rehabilitation in chronic stroke patients, looking at arm swing angle, gait, trunk control and postural stability.[7][8][9] A 2023 paper compared three wearable brassiere braces designed to correct rounded posture.[10] A Nepalese study compared a clavicle brace with plate fixation for displaced mid-shaft clavicle fractures.[11]
